messages: Rest a moment. Even Socrates slept.
Your resolve has been restored.
Sit down, catch your breath. The arguments will keep.
Your resolve has been restored.
A clear head wins debates. Let me help.
Your resolve has been restored.
Welcome to the Debate Arena!
Here you can rematch any philosopher you have previously debated.
Each rematch earns XP and can unlock concepts you may have missed.
Welcome to town. The Ethics Garden is through the southeast gate — Aristotle and Professor Wolf are in there.

Kant, Mill, and Singer hold the plaza; Rachels and Srinivasan are about too. Beat Wolf for the Ethics badge and the world opens: the far fields, the Academy northwest, the cave beyond it, and at last the cove.
The houses down south will patch you up between debates.
Immanuel Kant. Tell me the maxim of your action, and I will tell you whether it could be a universal law.
Most cannot.
You have reasoned for yourself. That, at least, the moral law demands of everyone.
John Stuart Mill. I have heard every objection to utilitarianism — the swine, the saint, the man with no time to calculate.
Bring me yours.
A fair hearing at last. Better Socrates dissatisfied, as I like to say.
Peter Singer. Before we begin: did you spend anything this week on something you did not need?
Then we have plenty to discuss.
You argue well. But the child is still in the pond, and we can still wade in.
James Rachels. People say morality is just cultural custom — that no society's code can be better than another's.
Shall we see whether that argument is actually valid?
Well argued. Remember: from the mere fact of disagreement, nothing follows about the truth.
Amia Srinivasan. Everyone here wants to maximize the good. Charming.
Ask me what their calculations leave out.
Good. Now go ask the same hard questions of your own side.
My roommate read one page of Kant and now nothing I do is universalizable.
They say the woman in the cove concedes your best premise and beats you anyway. I'd stay out of the water.
The forest north of here is quiet. Good for thinking — or for being ambushed by a thought.
Buy something or refute me. Those are the options.
Past this gate lie the Free Will Fields. They open once you hold the Ethics badge.
The garden gate is just ahead. Mind the philosophers in the tall grass.
The cave northwest gives me the creeps. A man in there says I don't know anything — and proves it.
We stock debate potions. Mill says higher pleasures only, but he still buys the cheap ones.
I moved out here to think for myself.
Then someone told me Hardwig proved that's overrated. Now I just chop wood.
Aristotle. You will not become wise by asking for a rule.
But a good argument is good practice. Come.
One swallow does not make a spring. Argue this well every day, and you may become good at it.
Susan Wolf. So you have debated the moralists and survived. One question remains.
Would you actually want to be the person their theories demand? Would you want to be friends with one?
Defend your ideal — not just its consistency, its attractiveness.
A life with room for both goodness and Tolstoy. You have earned the Ethics badge — the southeast gate out of town now opens to the Free Will Fields.
Professor Wolf planted this garden. She says a life needs more than moral flowers.
Aristotle keeps telling me my pruning shows promise but lacks habituation.
Jean-Paul Sartre. You tell yourself you had no choice in coming here.
There is always a choice. Refusing to admit that is bad faith, and I will prove yours to you.
You chose your argument freely, and it made you what you are. Remember that the next time you reach for an excuse.
Thomas Nagel. Two drunk drivers set out for home; a child steps in front of one of them.
You blame that one more. By your own principles, you shouldn't. Shall we sort this out?
Well argued. Though notice: whether you won this debate depended partly on which arguments happened to occur to you.
P. F. Strawson. Suppose someone proved to you tonight that determinism is true.
Would you stop resenting betrayal? Could you? I say the question answers itself — and that your whole free-will worry dissolves with it.
Quite so. The web of human attitudes holds us whether or not the theorists approve. The Freedom badge is yours — the Academy northwest of the town plaza will admit you now.
People come out here to resent things properly. Professor Strawson insists it's healthy.
Edmund Gettier. I wrote three pages once. They were enough.
You believe something true, with good justification — and I say you still may not know it. Care to defend your definition?
Ten coins, two cases, no survivors. Do give Smith and Jones my regards.
John Hardwig. Name one thing you know about physics, medicine, or history that you checked for yourself.
Thinking for yourself is a romantic myth — the rational move is usually deference. Prove me wrong, if you dare rely on your own arguments.
Notice what just happened: you cited authorities to refute me. I rest my case — and congratulate you.
C. Thi Nguyen. You think you'd know if you were in an echo chamber.
That is exactly what someone in an echo chamber would think. The corruption runs through your trust, not your information — and from the inside, you cannot tell.
Good. Now audit your trust, not just your feed. The exits are rarely where they appear to be.
Alvin Goldman. My colleagues in this cave have told you that you depend on experts, that your trust may be corrupted. All true.
But I say the novice can still choose rationally between rival experts — and that in the end only truth matters. Defend another goal if you can.
Truly argued — in the veritistic sense. The Knowledge badge is yours; the east trail from the Academy now leads to the Cove.
Thrasymachus of Chalcedon. Spare me the pieties about justice.
Justice is the advantage of the stronger, nothing more — and the just man everywhere comes off worse. Refute me, if you can do better than Socrates.
Hmph. You argue better than the flatterers. But look around the agora and tell me the strong are not still writing the rules.
Isaiah Berlin. Everyone who has promised to liberate your 'real self' has ended by coercing the self you actually are.
That is no accident. It follows from the idea itself. Convince me otherwise.
A fair fight. Remember only this: the great goods genuinely conflict, and whoever promises their final harmony is preparing a sacrifice.
Philip Pettit. Nobody interferes with Nora. Her husband indulges her completely.
I say she is unfree all the same — and if freedom is mere non-interference, you must say the contented slave of a kindly master is free. Will you?
Good. Now go look the world in the eye — without fear, without deference. That is what freedom is for.
Iris Marion Young. Show me the tyrant oppressing anyone here. You cannot — and yet the oppression is real.
Your theory of justice counts who gets what and misses all of it. Let me show you what it cannot see.
Well fought. But structures do not fall to good arguments alone — notice, next time, who cleans this agora after we leave.
John Rawls. You are proud of what you have earned. But your talents came from a lottery you did not enter, and your discipline from a home you did not choose.
Tell me, then: what exactly did you deserve?
That was fairly argued — a small original position, right here. The Justice badge is yours; the cave northwest of town stands open.
Rawls holds court at the north end. Bring arguments, not credentials — he says you didn't earn those.
I told Thrasymachus justice matters and he asked what it's paying me.
Professor Berlin has two words for every freedom you think you have.
I've read Republic Book One three times. Socrates wins on points but Thrasymachus wins the room.
The veil of ignorance ruined my scholarship essay. I couldn't stop asking who I'd be if I weren't me.
Pettit asked whether my landlord COULD evict me on a whim. Interfering isn't the point, apparently.
Professor Young says I should stop looking for the villain and check the org chart.
Study tip: never grant Thomson a premise. Not one. Not even a small one.
The library's closed. An echo chamber, they said. Something about corrupted trust.
I asked which expert to believe and got handed a paper called 'Experts: Which Ones Should You Trust?' Very funny.
Exams next week. If knowledge really is justified true belief, I'm two conditions short.
The east trail leads down to the cove. Final unit territory — they don't let you through without four badges.
Iris Marion Young made me count the five faces of oppression on my fingers. I keep a thumb free, just in case.
Berlin says the great goods conflict. So do my Tuesday lectures.
A student went into the cave certain he knew things. He's still in there, counting coins in his pocket.
The gardener claims Wolf's roses are supererogatory. Nobody corrects him; he seems happy.
Nguyen's seminar was full, so I just listen to people who agree with me. Wait.
Alastair Norcross. Meet my friend Fred. He tortures puppies in his basement — for gustatory pleasure he cannot otherwise obtain.
You are appalled. Then explain to me, precisely, how your lunch differs.
Well argued. Fred sends his regards — he says he'll see you at dinner.
James Rachels again. We settled cultural relativism; now medicine's dearest doctrine.
Smith drowns his cousin; Jones watches his cousin drown. If there is no moral difference there, the killing/letting-die distinction is finished — and with it, half of medical ethics.
Just so. Sometimes letting nature take its course is the crueler act. Doctors, of all people, should not hide behind it.
Peter Singer. I told you I would ask you to draw the circle wider. Here we are.
You grant equality to every human regardless of intellect or ability. On what principle, then, do you deny it to every other creature that can suffer?
The circle widens whether we bless it or not. You have argued honestly — the Equality badge is yours. One examiner remains, across the cove.
Judith Jarvis Thomson. You wake up plugged into a famous violinist. He dies if you unplug; nine months and he is saved.
I grant, for argument's sake, everything my opponents claim — and say you may still unplug. If I am right, the standard argument on this topic collapses. Final examination. Begin.
You may unplug — and you may argue. The final badge is yours. The Academy is proud; the semester, I believe, is won.
